title: Free Range Offline and On
author: Peter Gray
summary: Drawing on his work founding the nonprofit Let Grow, Peter Gray argues that the same over-protective instincts that restricted children's outdoor independence starting in the 1980s are now being applied to the digital world, and the consequences will be equally damaging. Research consistently disputes the idea that there is an overall clinically meaningful causal relationship between smartphone or social media use and children's mental health; increased academic pressure is a better-supported explanation for the mental health declines beginning around 2010. Children are growing up in the digital age, and denying them freedom to play and explore online is no less constraining on their development than denying outdoor freedom. 'Free range' does not mean unprepared — parents and communities have obligations to inform children about dangers, reduce hidden hazards, and hold media companies accountable. The overriding goal is to empower children rather than disempower them, helping them feel strong, resilient, and capable of enjoying digital life while minimizing genuine dangers.
points: The same over-protective instincts that restricted children's outdoor independence starting in the 1980s — contributing to increased anxiety and depression — are now being applied to the digital world, with predictably similar consequences.

Research continuously disputes the idea that smartphones or social media are a major overall cause of children's mental health decline; increased academic pressures (including Common Core) are better supported as explanations for the declines beginning around 2010.

Children are growing up in the digital age, and denying them freedom to play and explore online is no less constraining on their development than denying outdoor freedom — the digital world and physical world are increasingly merged.

Free range does not mean sending children unprepared: parents should inform children about dangers, communities should remove hidden hazards, and media companies must be held accountable for pornography, gambling-adjacent features, and addictive design.

The distinction between risks and hazards matters: risks are obvious and can be accepted or avoided; hazards are hidden and must be reduced; children need exposure to manageable risks to develop courage and learn to manage disappointment.
quotes: From the beginning, Let Grow has been dedicated to creating more freedom for kids to play and explore independent of direct adult control and monitoring.

Research has continuously disputed the idea that there is an overall clinically meaningful causal relationship between kids’ uses of smartphones or social media, or screens in general, and their mental health.

Children are growing up in the digital age. The digital world is as much a part of today's 'real world' as is the physical outdoor world. That is not going to change It's only going to become more true.
To deprive children of freedom in the digital world is no less constraining on their development than is depriving them of freedom in the outdoor physical world.
We do not do children a service by denying them the opportunity to explore in both spaces, nor do we do them a service if we deny or blind ourselves to the dangers in both spaces.

our goal as parents should be to empower our children, not disempower them; help them understand the dangers and help them realize they are strong, resilient, capable and can enjoy their online explorations and play while minimizing the dangers.

There is a difference between risks and hazards. Risks are dangers that are obvious, aboveboard. Because you can see them, you can choose to accept them a challenges or avoid them. Hazards are dangers that are hidden or not likely to be noticed.
